sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Reformist Phase**: Focused on **Abolition of Sati (1829)**, **Widow Remarriage (1856)**, and **Age of Consent (1891)**, driven by male reformers like Raja Ram Mohan Roy and Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.
• **Institutional Phase**: Emergence of women-led organizations like **Bharat Stree Mahamandal (1910)** and **Women's Indian Association (1917)** to demand suffrage and education.
• **Rights-Based Phase**: Post-1947 shift toward **Constitutional Equality (Art 14, 15)** and specific legislation like the **Hindu Succession Act (1956)**.
• **Key Metric**: The transition from 'protectionist' legislation (colonial) to 'empowerment' legislation (post-independence).

items.definition: Raised the age of consent for girls from 10 to 12 years. Opposed by Tilak on grounds of interference in religious customs.
Founded by Margaret Cousins; initially focused on education, later expanded to social reform and political rights.

items.title: Major Applications / Initiatives
items.content:
• **Suffrage Movement**: Women's organizations lobbied the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms for voting rights.
• **Legal Codification**: The Hindu Code Bill (1950s) was the most significant legislative overhaul for women's property and marriage rights.

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content:
• **Challenges**: Patriarchal resistance, lack of implementation of laws, and the 'private vs public' sphere divide.
• **Solutions**: Gender budgeting, mandatory representation in local bodies (73rd/74th Amendment).

items.title: Mnemonic for Retention
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym**: 'S-W-A-H' (Sati, Widow, Age, Hindu Code).
• **Decoded Meaning**: Sati (1829) -> Widow Remarriage (1856) -> Age of Consent (1891) -> Hindu Code Bill (1955/56).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often confuses the 'Age of Consent Act' (1891) with the 'Sarda Act' (1929). Sarda Act raised the marriage age to 14 for girls and 18 for boys.
Mains Value Addition: Use the term 'Substantive Equality' instead of just 'Equality' when discussing the Hindu Succession Act.

keyTakeaways: Legislation evolved from colonial 'social reform' to post-colonial 'rights-based' frameworks.
Women's organizations were instrumental in linking the 'Women's Question' with the 'Nationalist Question'.
The Hindu Code Bill remains the cornerstone of post-independence gender justice.
